content: For many years, intravenous sodium bicarbonate has been administered to counteract acidosis during the resuscitation of newborns. However, its use remains controversial. Most of the available evidence supporting its use comes from studies conducted on animals, adult humans, or uncontrolled and descriptive experiments. Despite the absence of robust evidence from studies specifically involving human neonates and concerns regarding its safety, some international resuscitation guidelines continue to recommend sodium bicarbonate for newborn resuscitation. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether administering intravenous sodium bicarbonate, compared to a placebo or no treatment, reduces mortality and morbidity in newborns undergoing resuscitation in the delivery room. Particular attention was given to its potential impact on neurodevelopmental outcomes. To address this, a comprehensive search was conducted using the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group's standard search strategy. Databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and CINAHL were searched for relevant studies up to September 2005. Additionally, Pediatric Research and conference proceedings from the American Pediatric Society/Society for Pediatric Research and the European Society for Paediatric Research were hand-searched for unpublished trials. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized or quasi-randomized controlled trials involving newborns who received sodium bicarbonate infusion during resuscitation in the delivery room. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials and extracted data. Study authors were contacted for additional information when necessary. Only one randomized controlled trial met the eligibility criteria. This study, conducted by Lokesh in 2004, compared the outcomes of asphyxiated newborns who required positive pressure ventilation at five minutes after birth. The intervention group (27 infants) received sodium bicarbonate infusion, while the control group (28 infants) received 5% dextrose. The study found no evidence that sodium bicarbonate infusion reduced mortality before discharge (relative risk 1.04, 95% confidence interval 0.49 to 2.21). Similarly, there was no significant effect on the likelihood of an abnormal neurological examination at discharge (relative risk 0.86, 95% confidence interval 0.30 to 2.50) or on the composite outcome of death or abnormal neurological examination at discharge (relative risk 0.97, 95% confidence interval 0.59 to 1.60). Furthermore, there were no statistically significant differences in the incidence of encephalopathy (relative risk 1.30, 95% confidence interval 0.88 to 1.92), intraventricular hemorrhage (relative risk 1.04, 95% confidence interval 0.23 to 4.70), or neonatal seizures (relative risk 1.19, 95% confidence interval 0.50 to 2.82). The study did not assess long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence from randomized controlled trials to determine whether the infusion of sodium bicarbonate during resuscitation in the delivery room reduces mortality or morbidity in newborns.
